Figure 4.13. Digestion and absorption of carbohydrates in the small intestine. 
Figure 4.13 Image Description 
Cartoon illustration showing major processes involved in digestion and absorption of 
carbohydrates in the small intestine. The figure shows starch and polysaccharides being 
digested down to maltose by pancreatic amylase; maltose digested to two glucose molecules; 
sucrose digested to one glucose and one fructose; and lactose digested to one glucose and 
one galactose. Monosaccharides are then absorbed into the bloodstream and travel to the 
liver. 
Fructose and galactose are converted to glucose in the liver. Once absorbed carbohydrates pass 
through the liver, glucose is the main form of carbohydrate circulating in the bloodstream. 
4 – Large Intestine or Colon 
Any carbohydrates that weren’t digested in the small intestine—mainly fiber—pass into the large 
intestine, but there’s no enzymatic digestion of these carbohydrates here. Instead, bacteria living 
in the large intestine, sometimes called our gut microbiota, ferment these carbohydrates to feed 
themselves. Fermentation causes gas production, and that’s why we may experience bloating and 
flatulence after a particularly fibrous meal. Fermentation also produces short-chain fatty acids, which
